entities.name: News of the World
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The News of the World, a British tabloid newspaper founded in 1843 by John Edward Taylor, emerged as a significant player in the realm of print media, particularly in Northern Europe. Headquartered in Wapping, London, it rapidly became known for its sensational journalism and celebrity gossip, reflecting and shaping public opinion during a transformative era in British history. As one of the longest-running newspapers in the UK, it held considerable influence over the national consciousness until its dissolution in 2011, marking an end to an era of tabloid journalism characterized by both innovation and controversy.

Throughout its operation, the News of the World was notable for its pioneering use of investigative journalism, with key stories including exclusive reports on high-profile crimes and scandals involving public figures. The newspaper reached its peak circulation in the 1970s, surpassing 8 million copies weekly, and was instrumental in the development of the tabloid format, which emphasized bold headlines and sensational stories to attract readers. However, it also faced numerous ethical challenges, particularly in the wake of the phone-hacking scandal that ultimately led to its closure, raising questions about media ethics and accountability.

The legacy of the News of the World is complex; it ushered in a new era of tabloid journalism that has influenced numerous publications worldwide, establishing trends in sensationalist reporting that persist to this day. Following its dissolution, discussions surrounding media ethics and regulation intensified, leading to inquiries into press conduct and a reevaluation of the relationship between the media and public trust. The impact of its closure is still felt, particularly as it spurred reforms within the British press and discussions about journalistic standards.
